claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature metastable BCC structure.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between a composition-dependent free-energy penalty for retaining BCC and kinetic nucleation barriers.
Solution thermodynamics and annealing temperature can govern phase stability and decomposition in Al–Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys.
A critical annealing condition can be predicted from CALPHAD free-energy calculations for Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Increasing annealing temperature or time beyond the critical condition causes the thermodynamic driving force to overcome the kinetic nucleation barrier.
Interfacial energies and changes in short-range order control local nucleation sites and mediate transformation of BCC into secondary phases.
Higher annealing temperatures increase the free-energy penalty for sustaining the high-temperature BCC phase.
Once the nucleation barrier is overcome, precipitates form and phase separation lowers the overall free energy.
Above a critical combination of temperature and hold time, secondary phases will nucleate and grow from an initially single-BCC matrix.
The fraction of secondary phases will increase with further annealing.
Lower-temperature annealing or insufficient holding time will preserve a single-phase BCC structure because nucleation barriers are not overcome.
The proposed transformation behavior is limited to temperatures and times near the calculated free-energy instability threshold.
At significantly lower temperatures or very short annealing times, the BCC phase will remain metastable.
Multicomponent high-entropy alloys exhibit thermodynamic and kinetic complexities, including sluggish diffusion kinetics.
Incremental annealing treatments bracketing the calculated threshold, with samples compared immediately below and above it, provide a controlled test.
Failure to detect any secondary phase or measurable microstructural change above the predicted threshold would falsify the proposed transition criterion.
